paras: The Westport hanging of two men was the discovery, reported on the evening of December 12, 1888, of the bodies of two unidentified men hanging from a tree near a school house south of Westport, in Jackson County, Missouri. Newspapers supposed the men were horse thieves lynched by farmers, vigilantes or an anti-horse-thief association, but no report named the dead or the men who hanged them. The item ran as a brief in papers from Minnesota and Kansas to California, Wisconsin, Dakota and Rhode Island over the following ten days.

According to a Kansas City dispatch of December 12, word came that evening from the village of Westport that two bodies had been found hanging to a tree near a school house "six miles south, or ten miles from Kansas City." The coroner left the city that night, though the dispatch warned that bad roads made further word unlikely before morning. A second Kansas City version, printed in Sacramento, said the men had been "hanged by vigilantes nine miles south of this city" and that the report was confirmed by a call for the coroner and two coffins.
A later dispatch said the county sheriff and coroner were called about twelve miles south of the city to view the bodies and "take proper action in the matter."

No report identifying the two men, giving the result of an inquest, or recording any arrest appears in the coverage. Missouri weekly news columns a week later still described the dead only as men found "a few days ago" six miles south of Westport, supposed to be horse thieves lynched by farmers.

The white press treated the case as a short wire item, and its headlines differed in how firmly they stated what had happened. The Wichita Eagle called it "A Rumored Lynching," while the St. Paul Daily Globe ran the same text under "Horse Thieves Hanged by Farmers," turning the wire's "supposition" into a headline statement. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed its version "Two Men Lynched" and attributed the hanging to "vigilantes."

In Wisconsin, Minnesota and Dakota the later dispatch appeared under headings such as "Anti-Horse Thieves at Work" and "The Anti-Horse Thief Association," with the remark that the association "has been doing a little work." The Superior Times reprinted the Watertown item word for word, and the Ste. Genevieve Fair Play carried the same Missouri news paragraph as the Iron County Register. By the time the story reached the Narragansett Herald on December 22, the dead were simply "two horse thieves" lynched by "a roving band of vigilantes."
None of the reports mentioned the race of the two men, and none questioned the supposition that they had been horse thieves.

Reports disagreed on the distance from Kansas City, giving six miles south of Westport or ten miles from the city, nine miles, and twelve miles. They also differed on who did it, naming farmers, vigilantes, or the Anti-Horse Thief Association, each as a supposition. A dispatch dated December 14 placed the officials' call on "last night," a day later than the same-day wires of December 12, which are the earlier and likelier date.

bases: Two unnamed men were found hanged from a tree south of Westport, and every report treated the deaths as a lynching of supposed horse thieves by farmers, vigilantes or an anti-horse-thief association (A1, A3, A9).

Two men were found dead hanging from a tree, and the papers supposed they were horse thieves hanged by farmers, 'vigilantes' or the Anti-Horse Thief Association (A1, A3, A6); no report gives witnesses, the size of the party, the men's identities or an inquest finding, so the lynching rests on supposition (A2, A11).

Two separate Kansas City wire versions on Dec. 12 (A1, A3) and a later Kansas City dispatch (A9) agree that two bodies were found hanging south of the city and that officials went to the scene, though the lynching itself is only supposed.
